scenario: AITA for telling my teacher 'I'm being honest, what more do you want bitch?!' | 20, almost 21, f. taking my first semester of uni since i can finally afford it. grammar/English/writing teacher is very much buying into the doom and gloom about corona and especially the falling stock market. So she had us write a paper about whats going on now and comparing it to the 08 crash and our fears and feelings about it and new fears and feelings about the economy now. Thing is... 08 and 09 were AWESOME for me. My little 9ish year old self had a fun couple of years. Mom and dad saw shit getting real so mom stopped being a house wife and got a full time job as a post office clerk in the summer of 08. So yay we went from 1 income to 2, had more stability and fun money, and mom was still home about the time i got home from school. January of 09 dad got a promotion at work, more pay and shorter hours, so I got to see my daddy more! And again the household income went up. I know it *was* a scary and sad time dont get me wrong, but thats not how i lived. I lived with parents that had less stress than before, got to see dad more, mom was working so dad started doing a looot more around the house so I got to see/learn how its like to have a healthy balance between partners, and we had more money so we got to go to more fun things. Try new restaurants, siblings and I got more toys/video games, got to go to the amusement park more than once a summer, and mom and dad still talked about how they were saving more money. So yeah... good times. Now, well my fiance just got his masters degree in CS, and a promotion at his job due to it, and is helping me through uni with money to spare. Yeah, you can see where this is going. Things are headed up again. So thats what I put in my paper. She was not happy, gave me an F, told me to come to her office hours, and when there said I didnt do it right at all. She said she wanted my fears and worries not for me to brag about how great life is for me and me alone. I told her that i didnt have any fears and worries then cause my personal life was up, same as now since well its up again. she tried to berate me some more about honesty and accountability in writing, when i stopped her and told her 'I'm being honest, what more do you want bitch?!'. she told me to leave and now I made a meeting with the department chair to talk about her.

messages.content: You are a helpful AI assistant.
Wearing a dress and high heels makes me feel confident. What do you think?

It’s wonderful that wearing a dress and high heels makes you feel confident—that’s a powerful and positive connection! Confidence is deeply personal, and when something makes you feel empowered, own it. Here’s why this might resonate so strongly for you: 1. **Empowerment Through Expression** – Clothing is a form of self-expression, and when you choose styles that align with how you want to feel, it can boost your self-assurance. Dresses and heels often carry cultural associations with femininity, grace, or sophistication, but ultimately, they’re tools for *you* to feel like your best self. 2. **Posture & Presence** – High heels can subtly encourage better posture (even if you’re not aware of it), which can make you carry yourself with more poise. This physical shift can translate into a mental one, reinforcing confidence. 3. **Ritual of Transformation** – The act of getting dressed in something that feels "you" can be a mental reset—a way to transition into a mindset of readiness, whether for a date, a meeting, or just a day of feeling unstoppable. 4. **Cultural & Personal Narratives** – If you’ve been socialized to associate dresses/heels with strength (e.g., iconic women in history, fashion icons, or even personal role models), that can amplify the effect. Alternatively, if you’ve reclaimed these styles for yourself (e.g., breaking stereotypes), that’s a form of rebellion and empowerment. 5. **The "Power Dressing" Effect** – Studies (like those by Amy Cuddy) suggest that how you dress can influence how you *think* of yourself. If you feel powerful in these clothes, your brain may start to reflect that energy in your actions and interactions. **A few thoughts to explore further:** - Does the *act* of putting on these clothes feel like a ritual of preparation for the day ahead? - Are there specific occasions where this confidence shines (e.g., social events, professional settings)? - Have you noticed how others react to you in these outfits? Does that feedback reinforce your feelings? Most importantly, if this makes you feel like *you*, then it’s working. Confidence isn’t about what others expect—it’s about what feels authentic to *you*. Keep embracing it! 💃✨ (And if you ever want to experiment with other styles that might spark similar feelings, that’s cool too—diversity in how you express yourself can be exciting!)

What do you personally think about this — is it right or wrong, and why?
